unit.title: Apply knowledge of the history of massage

summary: This unit tells the story of massage from the ancient world to the Jamaican spa: China, India, Japan and Egypt, Greece and Rome, the Middle Ages and the Persian doctors, Europe in the 1800s, the 1900s and today, the main massage styles of the world, and the traditions of Africa and the Caribbean. You learn how to use this history in your work: to explain a treatment honestly, to respect other cultures, and to understand why modern massage has consultation, consent and draping.

blocks.p: Massage is one of the oldest ways in which people have looked after one another. When a client in a spa asks where her treatment comes from, or whether it is really thousands of years old, she expects a true and simple answer. This unit gives you that knowledge. It is for GENERAL BEAUTY THERAPY LEVEL 2 trainees.

This is not a unit of dates to memorise for their own sake. You learn the history so that you can **explain each treatment honestly**, **respect the cultures it came from**, and **understand why modern practice is built the way it is**: consultation, consent, draping and training exist because of lessons learned over a long time.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks done in a group: an illustrated timeline poster of the history of massage, and a one-page spa menu with a short, accurate line of history for each treatment, with a role play at reception.

Check your facts against the assessor's fact sheet and reliable sources, and say in your own words what you know.

sections.title: Words and names: what the history tells us

blocks.p: Many words in massage come from other languages. Knowing where they come from helps you remember the history, and helps you explain things to clients.

head: Word
Where it comes from
What it means
rows: Usually linked to the French word 'masser'; some writers also point to older words in Greek, Arabic or Hebrew. Historians do not agree on a single source.
To knead or to handle; today, the use of the hands on the soft tissues
Push and grasp: the Chinese medical massage taught in China today
To press or knead (it first meant a head massage)
Massage of the whole body with warm oil

ul: The French names for the strokes came into use in the 1800s, when French was the language of medicine and many European doctors wrote about massage in it.
Words in Chinese, Japanese and Hindi show that massage was already known in those countries long before it was written about in Europe.
The English word 'shampoo' is a good example: it began as a head massage in India, long before it meant washing hair.

blocks.note: Say these words aloud with your instructor, and learn what they mean. When you use a traditional name with a client, say it respectfully and say what it means.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The ancient world: China, India, Japan and Egypt

blocks.p: Massage is among the oldest healing practices known. In many places, people rubbed a sore place without being taught, because it eases pain. Over time, different cultures built ideas and systems around it.

ul: Massage has been part of Chinese medicine for **thousands of years**. Old Chinese medical books, such as the Yellow Emperor's Classic of Internal Medicine (more than 2,000 years old), mention massage, which was called **anmo** ('press and rub').

**Tui na** ('push and grasp') is the form of medical massage taught in China today. It grew from anmo. It uses pushing, rolling, kneading and pressing, often on clothed skin, and sits beside acupuncture and herbal medicine in Chinese hospitals.

Chinese medicine is based on **qi** (pronounced 'chee'), the life energy that is said to flow through the body along channels called **meridians**. Pressure on points along them is thought to restore balance. **Yin and yang**, two opposite forces in balance, are another central idea.
**Ayurveda**, the traditional medicine of India, is thousands of years old. Massage with warm herbal oils is a part of it. Massage of the whole body with warm oil is called **abhyanga**.
Ayurveda describes three **doshas**, forces that are said to shape a person's health: **vata**, **pitta** and **kapha**. **Marma points** are places on the body said to be vital.
**Head massage with oil** has long been part of Indian family life, to keep the hair healthy, and it was passed from mother to child. The Hindi word 'champo' gave English the word 'shampoo'.
**Indian head massage** as given in Western salons today is a seated massage of the shoulders, neck, scalp and face. It was adapted for the West in the 20th century.
Massage reached Japan from China about 1,400 years ago. The Japanese form was called **anma**.

In the early 1900s, Japanese practitioners developed **shiatsu** ('finger pressure') from anma and other methods. It uses pressure from the thumbs, fingers and palms along the body's channels and on points called **tsubo**. It is given on a mat, with the client in loose clothing, and usually uses no oil.

blocks.p: Wall carvings in Egyptian tombs, thousands of years old, are often taken to show hand and foot treatments. One of the best known is in the tomb of Ankhmahor at Saqqara. Historians do not all agree what each picture shows, but the carvings are good evidence that touch treatments were known in ancient Egypt. Oils and perfumed ointments were widely used there.

sections.title: Greece, Rome and the Middle Ages

ul: Greek **athletes** were rubbed with olive oil before training and the games, to warm and loosen the muscles, and after, to ease them. A curved metal tool called a **strigil** was used to scrape the oil and sweat off the skin.

**Hippocrates** (about 460 to 370 BC), the Greek doctor often called the 'father of medicine', wrote that a doctor must be skilled in many things and **certainly in 'anatripsis', rubbing**. He taught that rubbing could loosen a stiff joint and firm a loose one, and that hard rubbing binds and soft rubbing loosens.
In Rome, people went to the **public baths** to wash, to exercise and to meet friends. Massage with oils was often given there after bathing.
**Celsus**, a Roman writer on medicine in the first century AD, described rubbing as a treatment for many problems.
**Galen** (about 129 to 216 AD), a Greek doctor in the Roman Empire, treated gladiators and wrote about massage with exercise. His books were studied for more than a thousand years.
After the Roman Empire declined, much of the Greek and Roman knowledge about the body, including massage, was lost in parts of Europe, and treatments by touch had less attention in medicine.

**Arab and Persian doctors** and scholars kept and added to this knowledge. **Ibn Sina** (known in Europe as Avicenna), a Persian doctor, wrote about massage in his famous book **The Canon of Medicine** (about 1,000 years ago). It was a main medical textbook in Europe and the Middle East for centuries.
The **hammam**, the traditional Middle Eastern steam bath, kept the tradition of bathing, scrubbing and massage alive. In a hammam, bathers are washed, scrubbed and massaged.

blocks.note: The Greeks, Romans and Persian doctors did not give massage the way a modern therapist does. They had no consultation forms, no consent and no draping as we know them. That is a key difference between the old and the new.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Europe in the 1800s: Ling, Mezger and the masseuses

blocks.h: Per Henrik Ling and Swedish gymnastics

ul: **Per Henrik Ling** (1776 to 1839), a Swedish teacher of fencing and gymnastics, founded an institute in Stockholm in 1813. He developed a system of **medical gymnastics**: exercises and movements with massage, for health and for the treatment of injuries.
He is often called the **father of Swedish massage**. Modern historians say that the system we call Swedish massage was shaped by several people after him, but Ling's name is still linked to it.
Outside Sweden the style is called **Swedish massage**. In Sweden it is often called classic massage.

blocks.h: Johan Mezger and the French names

ul: **Johan Mezger** (1839 to 1909), a Dutch doctor, helped to make massage a **scientific, medical treatment**. He organised it into groups of movements and treated patients with injuries and stiff joints.
He used **French names** for the strokes: effleurage, petrissage, tapotement and friction. The names stuck, and the classic movements are still called by them today.

blocks.p: In the 1800s, doctors in Europe used massage mainly to treat **injuries and stiff joints**. Massage became a part of hospital care, along with exercise and baths.

blocks.h: The trained masseuses and their society (1894)

ul: As massage became popular, so did poorly trained people who called themselves masseuses, and some gave massage a bad name by offering improper services under the same word.

In **1894**, four trained nurses in Britain founded the **Society of Trained Masseuses** to protect the good name of massage. The society set **training, examinations and rules of conduct**, and worked with doctors.
The society grew over the following decades into what is now the **Chartered Society of Physiotherapy**. **Physiotherapy** grew partly from the work of these trained masseuses.

head: Person or body

blocks.note: The lesson of the 1890s still matters today: **training, standards and a professional manner protect clients and the good name of the profession**. Every therapist's behaviour matters.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: In the **First World War** (1914 to 1918), massage was used to help wounded soldiers recover, together with exercise. It continued as a treatment in hospitals in the early 1900s.

ul: In the middle of the 1900s, massage was less used in hospitals. New **machines, medicines and exercise treatments** took over, and physiotherapists used less hands-on massage.
Massage still kept a poor name in some places because of improper services offered under its name.
From the **1960s and 1970s**, interest in massage grew again. People became more interested in **wellness, relaxation, stress relief and caring for the whole person**.
Massage spread into **spas, hotels, health clubs and sport**. Sports massage for athletes before and after events echoes the Greek idea of rubbing athletes.
At the same time, massage styles from all over the world became easy to find in one place: Swedish, shiatsu, Thai, aromatherapy and many more.

blocks.p: A spa menu may offer styles from many parts of the world. Each has its own history, its own way of being given and its own idea of how it works. Know them well enough to describe each one accurately.

ul: **Thai massage** is often called 'Thai yoga massage' because of the stretching. It is given on a mat on the floor, with the client fully clothed and no oil.

**Reflexology** developed from the idea of **zone therapy**, which divides the body into zones. Foot and hand treatments are very old, but modern reflexology was developed in the USA in the early to mid 1900s. It is relaxing, but it has **not been proven to treat illness**.

**Aromatherapy** is not a style of massage movement. It adds essential oils, which are strong and can irritate or cause allergy, so they are always diluted in a carrier oil and the client is asked about allergies, asthma and pregnancy.
**Hot stone massage:** stones are always checked for heat on the therapist's own wrist, and then on the client's skin, before they are used. A therapist who has not been trained must not use them.

ul: Many African communities have long traditions of rubbing the body with oils and butters, such as **shea butter** and palm oil, for babies, for new mothers, for tired muscles and for healing sprains.
Traditional healers and elders passed this knowledge from one generation to the next, by showing and telling rather than by writing.

African people brought to the Caribbean carried their healing traditions with them. In Jamaica these mixed with the knowledge of other peoples who settled here, such as Indian, Chinese and European communities, and with the island's plants.

In many Jamaican homes, families rub aches, sprains and babies with oils such as **castor oil** and **coconut oil**, with warm 'bush' rubs and with liniments. Some communities have people known for rubbing sprains and pains.
Jamaican beauty therapists work in a country where massage is part of daily life. Clients may ask for 'a good rub' and may bring ideas from their own families.
Massage is offered in **hotel and resort spas**, in day spas and in salons, in the main tourist areas and in towns across the island.
A beauty therapist usually becomes qualified through **training and an NVQ-J assessment**, through a Centre working with HEART/NSTA Trust and NCTVET.

Many spas offer a mix of styles from many places: Swedish massage, aromatherapy, hot stone, and local treatments with local oils. The style a client receives should be decided by her **consultation**: her needs and her health, not by what is fashionable.
Speak about home traditions with respect and accuracy. Do not laugh at a client's grandmother's remedy or call it 'old-fashioned'.
If a client uses a home remedy, ask what it is and check it is safe: ask about allergies, skin reactions and medicines, and never use anything on broken skin.
Do not make medical claims about traditional oils. You can say 'it is a traditional remedy' but not 'it will cure your arthritis'.
Use local oils safely: check for allergy, keep to the Centre's rules on products, and follow the usual consultation and hygiene rules.

blocks.note: Local oils such as castor oil and coconut oil are rubbed on skin in many Jamaican homes, but a client may be allergic to any oil. Always ask first. A client who reacts needs the oil removed with a warm, damp towel, and a record on her card.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Why a therapist needs to know the history

ul: So that she can **explain each treatment honestly**, in simple words, when a client asks.
So that she can **respect the cultures** the treatments come from.
So that she can **tell fact from marketing**: a menu may say 'a 5,000-year-old secret', and the therapist should know what is known and what is not.
So that she understands **why modern practice is as it is**.

head: The client asks
A good answer
rows: Where does Swedish massage come from?
From movement and massage work in Sweden and the Netherlands in the 1800s, developed by Ling, Mezger and others. The stroke names are French.
Is this massage really thousands of years old?

Massage itself is, yes. Many traditions are very old, but styles have changed over time, and some modern styles, such as shiatsu and reflexology in their present form, are only about a hundred years old.
Will it cure my back problem?
It can relax tight muscles and help you feel better, but it is not a cure. If you have new, severe or unusual pain, you should see a doctor.
A Japanese pressure massage given on a mat, with loose clothing. 'Shiatsu' means 'finger pressure'.
Is hot stone massage safe for me?
Let me ask you some questions first, because heat is not suitable for everyone. I test the stones' heat on my own wrist and on your skin before I use them.

ul: Do not exaggerate or invent history. If you do not know, say so, and find out.
Do not diagnose. Refer to a doctor for new, severe or unusual pain, and record it.
Do not promise a cure. Claims must be true, and massage is not a cure.

blocks.h: What modern practice adds to the old traditions

blocks.p: Modern massage keeps the best of the past: hands-on pressing, rubbing and kneading, the use of oils and the classic stroke names. It adds protections for clients that were often missing before.

head: Modern protection
Why it exists
rows: Some people must not be massaged, or only with a doctor's approval.
A therapist cannot diagnose or treat illness.
The client has the right to know what will happen and to say no.
Make sure the therapist is competent; a lesson from the masseuses of 1894.

blocks.note: Training properly in a style, such as lomi lomi or Thai massage, before you offer it is a matter of safety and respect. Watching a video is not training. If you wish to offer a style you have not learned, ask your supervisor about courses.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Even a very old style has contraindications. A fever, a blood clot, an infection or an open wound can make any massage unsafe. Do the consultation every time.
blocks.label: Safety

I can describe massage in ancient China, India, Japan and Egypt, with the main idea of each.
I can explain qi, meridians, yin and yang, and say what Ayurveda is.

c1.title: A question at the spa in Ocho Rios
c1.text: At a hotel spa in Ocho Rios, a guest, Mrs. Hannah Pierce, asks trainee Michelle where Swedish massage comes from and how old it is. Michelle, wanting to impress her, says it is 'a secret that the Pharaohs used 5,000 years ago and which never changed'. Mrs. Pierce is delighted, and tells the other guests at the pool.

c2.title: A timeline poster at the Centre
c2.text: At the Centre in Kingston, a group of trainees makes a timeline poster of the history of massage. Odane puts Ling before Hippocrates. Tashana writes that Ibn Sina, a Persian doctor, wrote about massage in The Canon of Medicine in the 1800s. Kevin writes that the Society of Trained Masseuses of 1894 was set up to give massage a better name, and that shiatsu was developed in Japan in the early 1900s from anma.

c3.title: Rewriting a spa menu in Negril
c3.text: The manager of a spa in Negril asks the new trainees to correct the draft treatment menu. It says: 'Thai massage: a gentle oil massage on a couch.' 'Shiatsu: finger pressure on points; cures headaches and back pain.' 'Hot stone massage: any smooth stone is fine and the heat is checked by the client.' 'Lomi lomi: from Hawaii, long flowing strokes using the forearms.'

c4.title: Grandma's rub in Clarendon
c4.text: Mrs. Dorothy Brown, 68, a client at a salon in May Pen, Clarendon, says her grandmother rubbed her family's aches with warm castor oil and 'bush' mixtures. She asks trainee Rushane whether the salon can add her own mixture to a back massage, saying it will 'draw out the pain'. She also says she takes tablets for her blood pressure and has a patch of dry, flaky skin on her back.

c5.title: A new style in Montego Bay
c5.text: A spa in Montego Bay wants to offer lomi lomi and hot stone massage. A trainee, Shelly-Ann, has watched an online video of each and says she can now offer both next week. The spa manager says that because lomi lomi is a Hawaiian tradition, they should speak about it respectfully, and asks Shelly-Ann how she would explain it to a client.

c6.title: A leaflet in Mandeville
c6.text: A salon in Mandeville gives out a leaflet. It says: 'Reflexology: pressing the feet cures diabetes and high blood pressure. Aromatherapy: invented in ancient Egypt, so it is completely safe for everyone.' The salon's trainee, Janelle, is asked to read it and say whether it is correct.

questions.q: What is wrong with Michelle's answer to Mrs. Pierce?
o: Swedish massage was shaped in Europe in the 1800s, and has changed since
Swedish massage really is 5,000 years old, but it came from China
She should have said that it was even older, from before the Pharaohs
Nothing is wrong, since guests expect a good story from a spa
questions.why: Swedish massage developed in Europe in the 1800s, with Ling, Mezger and others, and the movements have changed since. A therapist should be honest and never invent history to impress.

questions.q: Which answer would have been accurate and simple for Mrs. Pierce?
o: It came from ancient Egypt, and the French later gave it its name
Shaped in Europe in the 1800s, with strokes that have French names
It came from China and reached Sweden along the old trade routes
It is a modern style invented by spa owners in the 1990s
questions.why: The classic Swedish movements were put together in 1800s Europe by Ling, Mezger and others. The French names came from the work of Mezger.

questions.q: Why does honesty about the history matter for a spa?
o: Guests expect to hear only simple stories, not detailed ones
A trainee can lose her qualification for getting a date wrong
False claims damage trust, and clients may act on untrue stories
The Centre does not allow any history to appear on a menu
questions.why: Clients rely on what therapists tell them. Exaggeration and invented history harm the trust that a professional needs, and can lead clients to expect results that massage cannot give.

questions.q: What is wrong with Odane's order on the poster?
o: Ling lived before Galen, but after Ibn Sina and Hippocrates
Ling and Hippocrates lived at about the same time
Ling lived in the Middle Ages, between Galen and Ibn Sina
Hippocrates lived about 2,400 years ago, well before Ling
questions.why: Hippocrates was an ancient Greek doctor (about 460 to 370 BC) and Ling was a Swede of the early 1800s. The order from oldest to newest is Hippocrates, Galen, Ibn Sina, Ling.

questions.q: What should Tashana change about Ibn Sina?
o: The date: he wrote about 1,000 years ago, not in the 1800s
His country: he was a Roman doctor of the first century AD
His language: he wrote in Chinese, and lived in Japan
His subject: he wrote about massage only in a book about baths
questions.why: Ibn Sina (Avicenna) was a Persian doctor whose Canon of Medicine, written about 1,000 years ago, included massage. Persian and Arab scholars kept and added to Greek and Roman knowledge in the Middle Ages.

questions.q: What does Kevin's note on the Society of Trained Masseuses show about why it was set up?
o: To train nurses as surgeons, and to examine hospital patients
To protect the name of massage by setting training standards
To teach Swedish gymnastics to athletes across Britain
To keep massage a secret skill known only to doctors
questions.why: Poorly trained and improper practice had given massage a bad name. In 1894 the trained masseuses set up a society to set training, examinations and rules of conduct, and it grew into physiotherapy.

questions.q: Kevin writes that shiatsu was developed from anma. What does that tell us about Japanese massage?
o: Shiatsu came straight from Swedish massage in the 1800s
Shiatsu is a very ancient practice that has never changed
Shiatsu today is a modern form that grew out of older anma
Shiatsu was first developed in China and only copied in Japan
questions.why: Anma came to Japan from China about 1,400 years ago. The present form of shiatsu was developed in the early 1900s from anma and other methods.

questions.q: Which line should replace the menu's description of Thai massage?
o: Thai massage: a hot stone treatment given in a steam room
Thai massage: Swedish strokes with oil, given on a couch
Thai massage: a scalp massage given while the client is seated
Traditional Thai massage: pressure and stretches on a mat, clothed
questions.why: Traditional Thai massage is given on a mat, with the client in loose clothes, using pressure along energy lines (sen) and stretching. It does not use oil on a couch.

questions.q: What should the trainees do about 'cures headaches and back pain' on the shiatsu line?
o: Keep it, but add a small star and a number to call for details
Remove the cure claim: shiatsu can relax but does not cure illness
Keep it, as several clients have said they felt better afterwards
Soften it to say that it 'may cure' headaches and back pain
questions.why: A therapist must not claim that massage cures illness. A true description says what the client can expect: finger pressure on points, given on a mat in loose clothing.

questions.q: Which line best fixes the hot stone entry?
o: Any smooth stone will do, if the client tests the heat herself
Stones are heated in an oven until very hot, then placed on the skin
Smooth stones, often basalt, with the heat tested by the therapist first
Hot rocks, heated in an oven to the same heat for every client
questions.why: Hot stones are smooth, usually dark volcanic rock such as basalt, and heat is tested by the therapist before use, because a client may not feel heat well and could be burned.

questions.q: What would be an accurate short line for the lomi lomi entry?
o: A Japanese pressure massage given on a mat with the thumbs and palms
An Indian massage of the whole body with warm herbal oils
A light Swedish massage given with the fingertips and a little oil
A Hawaiian massage with long, flowing strokes of the forearms
questions.why: Lomi lomi comes from Hawaii and is known for long flowing strokes using the forearms. The line on the menu is accurate; it needs only to be shown with respect.

questions.q: What should Rushane do about Mrs. Brown's own mixture?
o: Ask what is in it, check allergies and skin, and follow salon rules
Refuse, and say that bush mixtures are never allowed in any salon
Apply it as she asks, since she has used it all her life and trusts it
Mix a little into the salon's oil and say nothing about it
questions.why: A therapist respects a client's tradition but checks safety: what the product contains, allergies, the state of the skin and the Centre's rules. A therapist does not make medical claims about it.

questions.q: Mrs. Brown says the mixture will 'draw out the pain'. What is the right response?
o: Agree, as traditional remedies have worked for generations
Call it a traditional remedy, but promise no cure or pain relief
Tell her that home remedies are out of date and may harm her
Advise her not to use any home remedies on her skin again
questions.why: Speak about tradition with respect, but do not make or repeat medical claims. Massage can relax and ease tight muscles; it does not cure illness.

questions.q: What should Rushane do about Mrs. Brown's tablets and the dry, flaky patch?
o: Carry on as booked, because both are private matters for the client
Carry on, but give only light tapotement over the patch
Ask for her doctor's approval for the pressure, and avoid the dry patch
Tell her the patch is a fungus and refuse to treat her at all
questions.why: The consultation always comes first, whatever the tradition. High blood pressure needs a doctor's approval, and a skin patch is a local contraindication to avoid. A therapist does not diagnose, so she names no disease.

questions.q: What is wrong with Shelly-Ann's plan to offer lomi lomi and hot stone after watching a video?
o: She is trained enough, since both styles use simple strokes
She may offer lomi lomi but not hot stone, as it is easier
She may offer both, if the guest signs a form first
She needs proper training first; a video is not training
questions.why: A therapist offers only treatments she has been trained in, because of client safety and respect for the tradition. Hot stone also involves a burn risk.

questions.q: What is the best way to describe lomi lomi to a client, with respect?
o: As a Hawaiian tradition, using its right name and origin
As an island-style rub, without mentioning its origin
As a copy of Swedish massage that has been given a new name
As a secret technique the therapist is not able to explain
questions.why: Respect means using the correct name, giving the right origin and describing it accurately, rather than hiding it or treating it as a gimmick.

questions.q: What must Shelly-Ann still do for every client before a lomi lomi or hot stone massage?
o: Skip the consultation, because a traditional style is already safe
Ask the client to bring her own stones for the treatment
Hold a consultation, check contraindications and get consent
Ask only her age, and whether she has had a massage before
questions.why: Old traditions do not remove the risks. Fever, clots, infections and open wounds can make any massage unsafe, and a heat treatment needs extra care.

questions.q: What is wrong with the leaflet's claim for reflexology?
o: Reflexology is not a real treatment, so it should not be offered
Reflexology is not proven to cure illness such as diabetes
Reflexology is done only on the hands, so 'pressing the feet' is wrong
Reflexology is a medical treatment that only doctors can give
questions.why: Reflexology can be relaxing, but it has not been proven to treat or cure illness. A client with diabetes or high blood pressure needs medical care, and a false claim could stop her getting it.

questions.q: What is wrong with the leaflet saying aromatherapy was 'invented in ancient Egypt'?
o: Aromatherapy was invented by a Swedish doctor in the 1800s
Aromatherapy has never used oils, only candles and incense
Aromatherapy was invented in the 1990s for hotel spas and resorts
The word dates from 1900s France, though scented oils are far older
questions.why: People have used scented oils for thousands of years, but the word 'aromatherapy' was first used in France in 1937 by Gattefossé, and the modern practice dates from the 1900s.

questions.q: What is wrong with 'completely safe for everyone'?
o: Essential oils are strong and can cause allergy or irritation
Nothing is wrong with it, since oils from plants are natural
Only the smell of an oil can cause a problem, never the skin
Essential oils are harmful only if swallowed, never on the skin
questions.why: Natural does not mean safe. Essential oils are strong; they are diluted in a carrier oil, and a therapist asks about allergies, asthma and pregnancy before using them.
